newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-RATIONALISATION LIFTS ADCOCK H1 SHR.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-RATIONALISATION LIFTS ADCOCK H1 SHR.

text.p: South African drugs group Adcock Ingram Ltd is expected to raise first half profits by between 12 and 20 percent as benefits from its rationalisation programme, started last year, kick in, analysts said.

"Their (Adcock's) earnings driver at the moment is going to be cost-savings. It looks like this is going to impact a little bit earlier than I expected," said a pharmaceuticals analyst who asked not to be identified.
Adcock is due to report results for the six months ended March 31 next Thursday.

Analysts said Adcock's rationalisation programme, which led to the closure of its consumer health care plant in the Indian Ocean port city of Durban and its Johannesburg-based self medication operation last year, could save the group between 50 and 100 million rand by the end of the year.
About 600 workers, including two directors, have been retrenched since late last year.
Analysts polled by Reuters forecast earnings per share at between 53.6 cents and 56.5 cents -- up from 47.2 cents a year ago. The consensus was at 55.0 cents.
They forecast a dividend of between 13 and 15 cents, with consensus at 14.3 cents -- up from the previous 12.6 cents a year ago.

Analysts said Adcock's earnings would also be helped by its tie-up with Premier Pharmaceuticals Ltd (Prempharm), which it bought last October raising its share of the South African pharmaceuticals market to about 15 percent.
Another boost would come from its critical care business which had seen better volumes.
However, a weaker rand during 1996 which lost 29 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar, is expected to weigh on some divisional performances, analysts said.
"It (the rand) probably hurt them. Their raw materials that come in are paid for in rands. But the general theme seems to be things are going fairly well," another analyst said.

Looking ahead, some analysts cautioned that although the second half was seen strong, government pressure that firms should embrace its primary health care plan by making cheaper medicines, could squeeze profit margins.
"There is quite a bit of pressure on margins with more emphasis being placed on cheaper medicines. I think it's quite tight for the manufacturers."
